nameStory: With a name like 'kiss-me-over-the-garden-gate,' this plant sounds like it belongs in a Victorian romance novel! The whimsical name comes from the way its long, drooping flower spikes seem to lean over garden fences, as if reaching out for a kiss from passersby. It's also called 'princess-feather' for those same elegant, plume-like blooms that nod gracefully in the breeze.
description: Kiss-me-over-the-garden-gate is a tall, graceful annual plant that can reach impressive heights in a single growing season. It's known for its distinctive drooping spikes of tiny pink or rose-colored flowers that hang like soft feathers or tassels. The plant has large, heart-shaped leaves and sturdy, upright stems that give it an almost tropical appearance. Originally from Asia, it's now found scattered throughout New England, though it's not particularly common here.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Long, drooping spikes of tiny pink flowers that hang like soft bottlebrushes or feathers, feeling fuzzy to the touch and measuring several inches long

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Large, heart-shaped leaves with pointed tips that feel smooth and soft, arranged alternately along the stem with visible leaf sheaths wrapping around the stem

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Tall annual that grows upright and can become quite robust, with multiple branching flower spikes that create a showy, almost exotic appearance

idTips.label: Stem
idTips.description: Sturdy, often reddish-tinged stems with swollen joints (nodes) that are characteristic of the knotweed family, feeling firm and smooth to the touch

habitat: In New England, kiss-me-over-the-garden-gate is most often found as an escape from cultivation near old gardens, roadsides, and disturbed areas. It prefers rich, moist soils and sunny locations, sometimes appearing in waste places or along fence rows where seeds may have been dispersed from nearby plantings.

seasonality.spring: Young plants emerge and grow rapidly, developing their characteristic heart-shaped leaves. The distinctive swollen stem joints become visible early.
seasonality.summer: The spectacular drooping flower spikes develop and bloom, creating the plant's most recognizable feature with their fuzzy, pink bottlebrush appearance.
seasonality.fall: Flowers fade and small, dark seeds develop. The entire plant begins to die back as cold weather approaches, being an annual species.
seasonality.winter: Plant dies completely, leaving only seeds to potentially germinate the following year. No above-ground parts persist through winter.

funFact: This plant was such a beloved garden flower in colonial America that it often appears in historical records of early New England gardens, yet today it's so rare in the wild here that it's been documented only 8 times by modern botanists!
confusionNotes: The drooping, feathery flower spikes are so distinctive that this plant is rarely confused with other species when in bloom. However, before flowering, the large heart-shaped leaves might be mistaken for other knotweeds, but the size and robust growth habit usually give it away.
contextualKnowledge: Despite its romantic English name, this plant is actually native to Asia and was brought to America as an ornamental garden plant. The 'orientalis' in its scientific name means 'from the east,' referring to its Asian origins.
compareHints: Among its knotweed relatives, kiss-me-over-the-garden-gate stands out dramatically with its large size and distinctive drooping flower spikes - most other Persicaria species have much smaller, upright flower clusters. While spotted lady's thumb and other smartweeds have tiny pink flowers too, they're arranged in short, upright spikes rather than the long, gracefully drooping plumes that make this species unmistakable.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Among New England's many smartweeds, low smartweed stands out for its distinctly bristly leaf sheaths and sprawling, ground-hugging habit - most other smartweeds grow more upright.

American jumpseed is unique among New England's Persicaria species for its woodland habitat preference - nearly all its relatives prefer sunny, wet areas like marshes, pond edges, or disturbed ground.
Among its smartweed relatives, arrow-leaved tearthumb is unique for its arrowhead-shaped leaves - most other Persicaria species have lance-shaped or oval leaves.

Among its many Persicaria relatives in New England, halberd-leaved tearthumb is unique for its climbing habit and distinctive leaf shape - most other smartweeds and knotweeds are upright plants with oval or lance-shaped leaves.
Far Eastern smartweed differs from spotted lady's thumb by having longer, more cylindrical flower clusters rather than short oval ones.
Among New England's many Persicaria species, water smartweed is unique in its amphibious lifestyle and dramatically different leaf forms.
Among its many Persicaria relatives in New England, spotted lady's thumb is one of the easiest to identify thanks to its distinctive dark leaf spots - most other smartweeds lack this feature.

Mile-a-minute differs from its native relatives like arrow-leaved tearthumb and halberd-leaved tearthumb primarily in leaf shape - it has equilateral triangular leaves while the others have arrow or halberd-shaped leaves with distinct pointed lobes.
Among New England's many Persicaria species, pinkweed stands out with its particularly dense, cylindrical flower clusters and robust growth habit.
Among New England's many Persicaria species, pale smartweed stands out for its consistently pale flowers - most other smartweeds have brighter pink blooms.
Among New England's many smartweeds, swamp smartweed stands out for its mild taste and preference for the wettest spots.
Among the many Persicaria species in New England, Asian jumpseed stands out for its delicate, thin growth habit and light green leaves with brown spots.
Among its many smartweed relatives, dotted smartweed is distinguished by those translucent leaf dots and its preference for very wet conditions.
Among its many Persicaria relatives in New England, waterpepper stands out for its intensely peppery taste and drooping flower spikes.
Among the many Persicaria species in New England, Nepal persicaria is distinguished by its relatively recent arrival and limited distribution.
Puritan Smartweed differs from other New England smartweeds by its preference for sandy rather than muddy habitats and its extremely limited distribution.
Carey's Smartweed differs from its common cousin spotted lady's thumb by having much sparser, more open flower clusters and lacking the dark triangular spots on the leaves.
Among New England's many Persicaria species, small water-pepper stands out for its truly diminutive size and exceptionally short flower clusters.
Among New England's smartweeds, bog smartweed's thread-like leaves are diagnostic – no other Persicaria species has such narrow foliage.
Among New England's many Persicaria species, Asian lady's thumb stands out for its low, mat-forming growth habit rather than the upright stance of most smartweeds.
Among New England's many smartweeds, stout smartweed lives up to its name with the thickest, most substantial stems in the genus.

Among New England's many Persicaria species, dense-flowered smartweed stands out for its exceptionally compact, bottlebrush-like flower spikes - much denser than the looser clusters of spotted lady's thumb or pinkweed.

Among New England's many Persicaria species, Japanese indigo is most similar to spotted lady's thumb and pinkweed in overall appearance, but it's much rarer and has a more upright, less sprawling growth habit.
